text:
Every lesson has a design section.

This is where you'll start designing a solution to a problem. It probably won't be perfect, but each lesson you'll make improvements. That's how engineers do it - piece by piece!

tiles.title: Who will your team design for?

text:
Read about the six people below, and choose one person who your team will design a specialized bionic arm for.

It might be easier to read this if you enlarge the screen. You can do that by hovering on the on the grey center line, and then clicking the arrows, like this:

objects.text: If you hover your mouse over the center, these arrow bars will pop up and you'll be able to enlarge the lesson side or the workspace side.
Icon alert! Whenever it's extra useful to enlarge the lessons side, you'll see an icon like this picture as a reminder!

text: Aisha is in college and she works in a chemistry lab with highly reactive chemicals. She wants to be a chemist when she graduates, and do research. Last year she lost her left hand in an car accident. Now she wants to get back to the lab - she might be a nerd, but she looooves working with chemicals. She is able to do a lot of regular daily tasks with the body-powered prosthetic she has (it closes when she extends her arm), but she realized she needs a specialized prosthetic for the lab. She needs to be able to hold beakers and test tubes in a way that the glassware won’t break, but very securely, so that they won’t fall under any circumstances.

Elliot lost their arm due to cancer when they were young. They used some prosthetics but they're all clunky and annoying, and Elliot has basically figured out how to do most things without one. But this year their parents got Elliot an iguana and they got really passionate about reptiles! They wants to be a herpetologist in the future (they have to tell everyone: that's someone who studies and works with reptiles) and they want to get prepared now! Right now Elliot only has Charles the iguana, but when they eventually work with a LOT of reptiles Elliot will need to be able to quickly and efficiently grab small reptile food, sometimes including live crickets or small pellets. It’s okay if they drops them sometimes, the main issue is just being able to pick them up – they’re small! Elliot needs to be able to do this while holding the reptiles in his other hand. They also don't want to crush the reptile food – it just makes everything messy. If they could hold a reptile with the bionic arm that would be a bonus, but for now Elliot wants to start with being able to feed them and do other reptile care.

Jayde has always been proud of her limb difference – she doesn’t want to be “fixed.” Her mom tells her she’s perfect exactly how she was born. It’s cliche, and lots of moms say that about their kid... but Jayde agrees. She's pretty awesome.

Jayde has been learning to do beadwork from her mom and grandma and she’s pretty good. It’s an important part of her culture, too. Now that she’s working on more complicated projects, and she’s working faster, she thinks a maybe bionic arm could be a useful tool to help. She’s actually not totally sure what exactly could help her, but she wants it to be something “extra.” She wants it to be different from what she could do with just a "replacement hand" – like how in sci-fi books people get cyber extensions.

Antoninho plays the guitar. His parents even named him after a musician, called Antoninho Travadinha! He plays a style of music called morna which keeps him connected with his family roots even though most of his aunts, uncles, and cousins live basically across the world... but he also likes being able to play stuff he listens to with his friends, like Bad Bunny songs. His left hand is still able to make the chords, it's totally fine. But he was in a really bad accident a couple years ago and his right hand was amputated almost up to the elbow, and his right arm sustained damage so he can’t move his elbow and his whole arm is pretty weak.

Antoninho has a body powered prosthetic that looks like a claw. He controls it by squeezing his left arm. It's fine for regular stuff like getting dressed and carrying stuff and whatever, and Antoninho likes that it has different attachments - it's not his old arm, but it's pretty okay... almost. The problem is, that prosthetic is definitely not working for his music. Because he can’t move his elbow, it requires him to move his whole arm up and down, but that is difficult and causing him pain. Music is a really big deal in his life and how he connects with his family and friends, and he wants a solution!

Miguel just turned four and a half! (He always tells people about the half now!) He was born without hands. He has used passive prosthetics so far -- the hands don't move unless he moves them, but they let him him hold things. Sometimes he likes it, sometimes he does NOT. His parents want him to figure out what works for him as he gets older, so they're letting him figure out how to do things with the prosthetics and without.

Next year, Miguel will be starting kindergarten. His physical and occupational therapists think it would be helpful if he could prepare to use his hand for school things. They recommend getting him bionic arms -- meaning, arms that respond to his muscle movements, and that actually open and close. Eventually they want him to be able to write, flip pages in a book, get dressed independently, and do anything else he wants, but right now his PT and OT think it would be a good idea to start with some bigger things, like learning to pick up a small cup or ball with just one hand, without having to use both hands for everything.

Vera is training to be a Berezka dancer. This is a kind of dancing where uniformity is very important – they all need to look the same. Vera has a passive prosthetic that looks kind of lifelike, but it doesn't move. It doesn’t really work well for this dancing, and honestly, she doesn't think it's a good fit for her anymore. When she first lost her hand she was really embarrassed about her stump and wanted to hide it, but her friends were super supportive, and her counsellor was, too. Now, she only wears her prosthetic if she needs it to do things, not just to look "normal." But for this kind of dancing, she doesn't want to stand out. She loves how everyone moves together. So for her bionic arm, she wants to be able to hold some light objects, like scarves or flowers, which are used in the dance, and to for her hand to move very smoothly based on what her arm muscles are doing.

An important part of engineering is iteration: trying things and improving it over time. You can probably think of a LOT of different motions and functions that would be useful for your person. Over time, you will make prototypes with more features, but you probably won’t figure it out all at once.

One way to start is to focus on something very specific.

What is one motion or action that you think is especially important for this person? Why did you choose to start with that motion?

tiles.title: Write the name of the person you picked here!

text: You can try writing: [Person's name] needs to be able to [make this motion]. This is a good motion to start with for [person's name] because _______________.

Here are a few designs for an initial prototype (the instructions will be in a handout that you will get later - right now you're not making them, you're first designing.

Decide which one your team will make, but also think about one improvement you can make to it that will be helpful for the person you chose.

It can be a big or small change, but it should be feasible - meaning, you should be able to actually make that improvement!

text:
How will you improve your prototype? You can...

1. Write your ideas

2. Drag the picture of the prototype and sketch over it

3. Draw your ideas on paper and take a picture
